full_judgment:
27. Section 101 of the Evidence Act, requires that the plaintiff who wants the Court to believe that the alleged receipts have created any right or title in his favour or any legal right or liability has been created by virtue of such settlement by way of those rent-receipts, it is the plaintiff who has to prove the same in a legal manner as provided under the Act. Whether these rent receipts were genuine or represented true and correct state of things, the burden of proving such things heavily lies on the plaintiff. It is to be noted that no witness has been examined to prove the rent receipts, the alleged signature of the Manager of the Tea Company Limited or the contents of such rent-receipts. Without such proof the rent-receipts Ext. 1, 1(a), 1(b) and Ext. 2 cannot be accepted as legally proved or exhibited. The learned Judge thus has committed a serious error of law in taking into consideration and based his decision on the rent-receipts in matter of title which 'affected the merit of the casco Mere filing a rent receipt or a private document without formal proof thereof and without proving the contents of such documents cannot fulfill the requirements of section 101 and section 103 of the Evidence Act. Therefore, in my view, by Ext. 1, 1(a), 1(b) and Ext. 2, the plaintiff has acquired no title. 

 "In this case the plaintiffs have come to the Court with the assertion that the disputed land was settled with them by the owners of the land on the basis of the Kabuliyat Ext. 3(a) and produced the Dakhilas Ext. 4 series in proof of the fact that the Kabuliyat was acted upon on subsequent payment of rent in pursuance of the said settlement. According to section 101 of the Act, as referred to above, it is for the plaintiffs to prove that as a matter of fact, settlement was granted by the owners of the land and the rent receipts Ext. 4 series were really genuine and represented the correct state of things, as the plaintiffs desire the Court to believe on the said assertion. The burden of proof as to the genuineness of the dakhila Ext. 4 series is undoubtedly upon them in the absence of any legislative provision to the contrary. There having been no legislative enactment requiring the dakhilas, Ext. 4 series, which had been formally proved at the trial of the suit, to be accepted as genuine documents, merely on proof thereof there is no question of shifting the onus upon the defendants. The learned Judges of the High Court appears to have been under a misapprehension as to the real effect of formal proof of a document in a Court of law. A private document cannot be taken notice of and marked as an exhibit without any formal proof, unless the requirement of such proof is waived by the opposing party. The marking of the said document as an exhibit may, however, give rise to a belief that it bears the writing or signature of a person as has been deposed to by the witness who proves the said document. The question as to whether the document is a genuine one or it represents the true state of affairs is a question of fact which is to be decided by the Court concerned in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case. There is no legal presumption which the Court is bound to make in respect of such a document. There may be cases where the law requires that the contents of a particular document shall be presumed to be correct unless they are rebutted by adducing evidence by a party who disputes their correctness, as has been provided in section I03B of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. There is no such law as requires a Court to presume that a rent receipt purported to be granted by a landlord in favour of a certain person is genuine and what has been written in such a rent receipt are true. The learned Judges of the High Court have apparently made a mistake in taking the view that as soon as the rent receipts have been proved the primary onus of the plaintiffs has been discharged and the defendants having failed to produce any rebutting evidence the said rent receipts should have been accepted as genuine and relied upon. The onus of the plaintiffs cannot be discharged until the Court is persuaded to accept the position that there had been payment of rent by the tenant and acceptance thereof by the landlord, as a matter of fact on the basis of the disputed rent receipts. In this case both of the Courts of fact have decided the question of genuineness of the disputed rent receipts in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and have also examined their various features with reference to the surrounding facts and came to the definite finding as to their spurious character. Such a finding is binding upon the High Court in a Second Appeal unless it could be shown the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or of procedure which had affected the merits of the case."
